```{r svm, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
  # complete.cases() check is needed here: df has already been
  # filtered to complete cases by preparer_niveaux() before
  # reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column (including the
  # dependent variable) to the [0, 1] range.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop.
  # Identical expanding-window logic to the MLR and Random
  # Forest loops: at each step, the SVM is refitted from
  # scratch on the initial training set plus all test rows
  # already passed, and a single prediction is generated for
  # the current test observation. cost and gamma are held
  # fixed at the values selected by the tuning chunk above
  # for every step of the loop.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    modele_svm <- svm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                      kernel = "radial", cost = cost, gamma = gamma)

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_svm, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# Uses the cost and gamma values selected by the tuning
# chunk above, separately for each series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_svm_ara <- fit_svm(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
                       cost = tuning_svm_ara$cost, gamma = tuning_svm_ara$gamma)
res_svm_rob <- fit_svm(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
                       cost = tuning_svm_rob$cost, gamma = tuning_svm_rob$gamma)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_svm <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara$actual, res_svm_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob$actual, res_svm_rob$predicted))
)
```

The SVM with a radial basis function kernel and tuned hyperparameters delivers strong out-of-sample performance. The light grid search selects $cost=5$ and $gamma=0.05$ for both Arabica and Robusta, the combination minimising validation MSE within the chronological 80/20 sub-split of each initial training window. With these tuned hyperparameters, the SVM achieves an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.813 for Arabica and 0.723 for Robusta, comparable to or exceeding several of the other ML models for both series. The single pre-loop tuning search remains a simplification relative to a fully nested walk-forward procedure, which would re-optimise the hyperparameters at every step but was computationally prohibitive given the sample size and the six-model comparative framework of this study.

## Artificial Neural Network (ANN)

*This chunk estimates the Artificial Neural Network model for both series using the `nnet` package, which implements a single hidden layer feedforward network trained by backpropagation. The number of hidden neurons is selected via a light grid search over candidate sizes of 3, 5, 8 and 10, using the same chronological sub-split of the initial training window as the SVM tuning procedure.*

```{r ann_tuning, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# LIGHT HYPERPARAMETER TUNING — ANN
# A chronological 80/20 sub-split of the initial training
# window is used to select the optimal number of hidden neurons
# from a small grid. The selected size is then held fixed
# across all walk-forward steps in the estimation chunk below.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

tuner_ann <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles  <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  df_modele             <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele             <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled      <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))
  donnees_train_complet <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  n_sous_train          <- floor(nrow(donnees_train_complet) * 0.8)
  sous_train            <- donnees_train_complet[1:n_sous_train, ]
  sous_val              <- donnees_train_complet[(n_sous_train + 1):nrow(donnees_train_complet), ]
  formule               <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))
  tailles_candidates    <- c(3, 5, 8, 10)
  mse_val               <- numeric(length(tailles_candidates))
  for (i in seq_along(tailles_candidates)) {
    set.seed(42)
    modele_essai <- nnet(formule, data = sous_train,
                         size   = tailles_candidates[i],
                         linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)
    preds_val    <- predict(modele_essai, newdata = sous_val)
    mse_val[i]   <- mean((sous_val[[var_dep]] - preds_val)^2)
  }
  meilleure_taille <- tailles_candidates[which.min(mse_val)]
  list(size   = meilleure_taille,
       grille = data.frame(size = tailles_candidates, mse_val = mse_val))
}

tuning_ann_ara <- tuner_ann(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
tuning_ann_rob <- tuner_ann(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)

cat("ANN - Arabica selected size:", tuning_ann_ara$size, "\n")
cat("ANN - Robusta selected size:", tuning_ann_rob$size, "\n")
```

*The selected architecture is passed directly to the estimation function below, which follows the same walk-forward expanding window structure as all other models.*

```{r ann, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(nnet)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#
# Architecture: one hidden layer with `size` neurons.
#   size   : selected by the tuning chunk above
#   linout = TRUE : linear (identity) activation on the output
#                   neuron, required for regression targets.
#                   Without this, nnet applies a logistic
#                   activation and predictions are constrained
#                   to (0, 1), which would be inappropriate
#                   even though the data is already scaled
#                   to [0, 1], since the model still needs to
#                   be able to predict slightly outside that
#                   range during the walk-forward loop.
#   maxit  = 500  : maximum number of backpropagation
#                   iterations before convergence is declared.
#
# Weight initialisation in nnet is random. set.seed(42) is
# called ONCE, immediately before the walk-forward loop starts
# (not inside the loop), so that the entire sequence of random
# weight initialisations across all walk-forward steps is
# reproducible from one run of this chunk to the next.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, size = 5) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model needs. No
  # complete.cases() check is needed here: df has already been
  # filtered to complete cases by preparer_niveaux() before
  # reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column (including the
  # dependent variable) to the [0, 1] range.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop.
  # Identical expanding-window logic to the MLR, Random Forest
  # and SVM loops: at each step, the network is reinitialised
  # and retrained from scratch on the initial training set plus
  # all test rows already passed. There is no warm-starting from
  # the previous step's weights, which would introduce a form
  # of temporal leakage across walk-forward steps.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  set.seed(42)   # fixed once, before the loop starts (see note above)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    modele_ann <- nnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                       size   = size,
                       linout = TRUE,
                       maxit  = 500,
                       trace  = FALSE)

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_ann, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_ann_ara <- fit_ann(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
                       size = tuning_ann_ara$size)
res_ann_rob <- fit_ann(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
                       size = tuning_ann_rob$size)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_ann <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara$actual, res_ann_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob$actual, res_ann_rob$predicted))
)
```

The light tuning search selects a hidden layer of 5 neurons for Arabica and 3 neurons for Robusta, the architecture minimising validation MSE within the chronological sub-split of each initial training window. With these tuned architectures, the ANN achieves an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.453 for Arabica and 0.441 for Robusta. For Robusta, the 3-neuron architecture selected by the tuning search performs relatively poorly out-of-sample. This outcome illustrates a genuine limitation of the single-split validation approach: the architecture that minimises error on the validation portion of the training window does not necessarily generalise best to the separate test period, particularly with a network this small and a validation sample of limited size. Rather than discarding the tuning result in favour of an alternative, which would amount to selecting hyperparameters based on test set performance and would violate the walk-forward validation protocol, the tuned size is retained as the methodologically consistent choice. This result is fully reproducible across repeated executions of the chunk, confirming that the fixed seed eliminates run-to-run variability and that the outcome reflects the architecture and validation procedure itself rather than random initialisation noise. The reduced capacity of the 3-neuron Robusta network, combined with the absence of explicit regularisation, leaves the model susceptible to converging on a comparatively poor solution within the limited number of backpropagation iterations, an outcome consistent with the known sensitivity of small feedforward networks to both architecture and weight initialisation.


## Comparative Performance Analysis

*This chunk consolidates the six individual metric data frames into a single comparison table and produces the summary bar chart. The metric columns are coerced to numeric here because `cbind()` in the individual model chunks stores them as character strings when binding with the Model and Series label columns. Two separate tables are rendered, one per coffee variety, to keep each readable, followed by a grouped bar chart that allows visual comparison of $R^2$ across all model-variety combinations simultaneously.*

```{r comparative_performance, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — COMBINE ALL MODEL METRICS
# bind_rows() stacks the six two-row metric data frames into
# a single 12-row frame (6 models × 2 series).
# as.numeric() coercion is necessary because cbind() in each
# model chunk coerces numeric columns to character when
# binding them with the Model and Series string columns.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_all <- bind_rows(
  metriques_mlr, metriques_arimax, metriques_rf,
  metriques_xgb, metriques_svm,   metriques_ann
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — SINGLE PERFORMANCE TABLE (ARABICA AND ROBUSTA)
# Models are sorted by decreasing R² within each series.
# The Series column is dropped before kable() to avoid
# conflict between collapse_rows() and pack_rows().
# MSE and MAE are rounded adaptively: large values (ARIMAX
# and MLR in original price units) are rounded to the nearest
# integer with a thousands separator; small values (ML models
# on the [0, 1] scaled range) retain four decimal places.
# pack_rows() adds colour-coded group headers for each series,
# making the Arabica / Robusta separation immediately visible.
# A footnote warns the reader that MSE and MAE are not
# directly comparable across the two model groups.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_all %>%
  arrange(Series, desc(R2)) %>%
  mutate(
    MSE = ifelse(MSE > 100,
                 format(round(MSE, 0), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
                 as.character(round(MSE, 4))),
    MAE = ifelse(MAE > 10,
                 format(round(MAE, 1), scientific = FALSE),
                 as.character(round(MAE, 4)))
  ) %>%
  select(Model, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Comparative model performance — out-of-sample results",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R²", "MSE", "MAE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(6, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 6,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 7, 12,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  footnote(general           = "MSE and MAE for ARIMAX and MLR are in original price units (USD/lb for Arabica, USD/tonne for Robusta). MSE and MAE for RF, XGBoost, SVM and ANN are on the Min-Max scaled [0, 1] range and are not directly comparable.",
           general_title     = "Note:",
           footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — COMPARATIVE R² BAR CHART
# Models are ordered by decreasing average R² across both
# series to place the strongest performers on the left.
# R² labels are displayed above each bar for readability.
# A dashed reference line at R² = 0.75 provides a visual
# benchmark distinguishing strong from weaker performers.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_all %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(Model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "XGBoost", "SVM",
                                   "Random Forest", "MLR", "ANN"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = R2, fill = Series)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge",
           alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 3)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.75, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Arabica" = "#8B4513",
                               "Robusta" = "#2E8B57")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.02),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(title    = "Out-of-sample R² by model and coffee variety",
       subtitle = "Dashed line at R² = 0.75",
       x = NULL, y = expression(R^2), fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1),
        legend.position    = "top",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The comparative results are summarised in the tables and chart above. The ARIMAX model emerges as the strongest single model for Robusta ($R^2 = 0.929$) and remains highly competitive for Arabica ($R^2 = 0.821$), confirming that the autoregressive structure of price dynamics is a powerful predictor. XGBoost is the strongest ML model for both varieties ($R^2 = 0.818$ for Arabica, 0.796 for Robusta), closely followed by SVM and Random Forest. The MLR benchmark performs well for Arabica but fails for Robusta, highlighting the importance of temporal dynamics in the shorter Robusta sample. The ANN produces the weakest results across both varieties, for the reasons discussed in the preceding section.

The walk-forward validation protocol ensures that all reported metrics reflect genuine out-of-sample forecasting ability, with no possibility of data leakage between the training and test periods. With the exception of the ANN, $R^2$ values remain above 0.75 across all model-variety combinations, suggesting that the predictor set constructed in this study captures meaningful information about the drivers of coffee futures prices.

### Variable Importance and Partial Dependence Plots

The variable importance plot from the Random Forest model provides an indication of which predictors contribute most to forecast accuracy, measured by the percentage increase in MSE when each variable is randomly permuted while holding all others fixed.

*The importance scores were recorded at the final walk-forward iteration, corresponding to the largest training window, and stored in the `importance` element of `res_rf_ara` and `res_rf_rob`. Internal variable names are recoded to the same display labels used in the correlation matrix and PCA plots for visual consistency. Bars are sorted in descending order of `%IncMSE` so that the most influential predictor appears at the top of each chart after the axis flip.*

```{r variable_importance, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}

library(tibble)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — EXTRACT IMPORTANCE SCORES
# importance() returns a matrix with one row per predictor
# and multiple importance metrics. rownames_to_column()
# converts the row names (internal variable names) to a
# regular column so they can be recoded and used in ggplot.
# Results are sorted in descending order of %IncMSE so that
# the most important variables appear at the top of the plot
# after coord_flip() reverses the axes.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

imp_ara <- as.data.frame(res_rf_ara$importance) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
  arrange(desc(`%IncMSE`))

imp_rob <- as.data.frame(res_rf_rob$importance) %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
  arrange(desc(`%IncMSE`))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — RECODE VARIABLE NAMES TO DISPLAY LABELS
# Internal column names from the dataset are replaced with
# the same English display labels used in the correlation
# matrix and PCA plots, ensuring visual consistency across
# all figures in the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

labels_vi <- c(
  "cot_net_mm"     = "COT net MM",
  "sugar_price"    = "Sugar",
  "ending_stocks"  = "Ending stocks",
  "wti"            = "WTI",
  "cpi"            = "CPI",
  "oni"            = "ONI",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "Fed Funds Rate",
  "production"     = "Production",
  "cocoa_price"    = "Cocoa",
  "exports"        = "Exports",
  "dxy"            = "DXY",
  "consumption"    = "Consumption",
  "indice_temp"    = "Temperature",
  "indice_precip"  = "Precipitation"
)

imp_ara <- imp_ara %>% mutate(Variable = recode(Variable, !!!labels_vi))
imp_rob <- imp_rob %>% mutate(Variable = recode(Variable, !!!labels_vi))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — HORIZONTAL BAR CHARTS
# reorder(Variable, `%IncMSE`) sorts bars from least to most
# important along the y-axis; coord_flip() rotates the chart
# so that the most important variable appears at the top.
# geom_text() adds the exact %IncMSE value at the end of
# each bar. panel.grid.major.y removes horizontal grid lines
# that would otherwise clutter the flipped chart.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Arabica importance plot
ggplot(imp_ara, aes(x = reorder(Variable, `%IncMSE`),
                    y = `%IncMSE`)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "#8B4513", alpha = 0.85,
           width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`%IncMSE`, 1)),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title    = "Variable importance - Random Forest (Arabica)",
       subtitle = "% increase in MSE when variable is permuted",
       x = NULL, y = "% Inc MSE") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"))


# Robusta importance plot
ggplot(imp_rob, aes(x = reorder(Variable, `%IncMSE`),
                    y = `%IncMSE`)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "#2E8B57", alpha = 0.85,
           width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(`%IncMSE`, 1)),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title    = "Variable importance - Random Forest (Robusta)",
       subtitle = "% increase in MSE when variable is permuted",
       x = NULL, y = "% Inc MSE") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"))
```

The variable importance plots reveal distinct predictor hierarchies across the two coffee varieties, while also highlighting a set of common drivers that transcend the specificities of each market.

**For Arabica**, Sugar No.11 prices and the COT net Managed Money position emerge as the two most influential predictors, contributing approximately 27% and 24% increase in MSE respectively when permuted, well above all other variables. Ending stocks rank third (approximately 20% Inc MSE), consistent with the theoretical role of inventory levels as a primary determinant of commodity prices. WTI and ONI follow at approximately 18% and 17%, with CPI and the Fed Funds Rate contributing approximately 16% and 15% respectively. The USDA fundamentals variables, Production, Exports and Consumption, occupy the middle range, likely penalised by their high mutual collinearity documented in the correlation and PCA analyses. Temperature and Precipitation rank last, contributing approximately 6% and 3% Inc MSE respectively, suggesting that their influence on Arabica prices at monthly frequency is either lagged beyond the one-step-ahead horizon or mediated through the supply and inventory variables already present in the model.

**For Robusta**, the importance hierarchy differs markedly in its upper ranks. WTI and CPI are the two dominant predictors (approximately 25% and 22% Inc MSE respectively), displacing the financial and market-specific variables that led the Arabica ranking. COT net MM ranks third (approximately 19%), followed by Cocoa (approximately 18%) and Ending stocks (approximately 18%). Production, ONI and DXY contribute between 15% and 16%, while Sugar and the Fed Funds Rate follow closely at approximately 15% and 14%. Temperature and Precipitation rank last at approximately 8% and 6% respectively, somewhat higher than their Arabica counterparts, which may reflect the greater sensitivity of low-altitude Robusta cultivation to temperature and moisture anomalies. As with Arabica, the ICE Futures Europe contract for Robusta is less actively traded than ICE Coffee C, which may explain the somewhat lower importance of COT net MM relative to the Arabica specification.

Across both varieties, financial and macroeconomic variables systematically outrank supply-side fundamentals and climate variables in terms of predictive contribution at monthly frequency. The climate variables contribute the least predictive power of any variable group. This does not imply that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices, but rather that its effects may operate primarily through supply with a lag of several months to a full growing season, a channel that a contemporaneous monthly model is not designed to capture. The implications of this finding are discussed further in the limitations section.

### Forecast Trajectories

*This chunk collects the actual and predicted values from all six models into a single tidy data frame, separately for Arabica and Robusta. This unified structure allows all forecast plots to be produced with a single `ggplot2` + `facet_wrap()` call rather than six separate plots. The test period dates are reconstructed from the levels datasets used during estimation, ensuring the x-axis of each plot reflects the correct calendar dates.*

```{r forecast_data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA — COLLECT PREDICTIONS FROM ALL SIX MODELS
# The test period starts at observation n_train_ara_lev + 1
# in df_arabica_levels. Dates are extracted from that dataset
# to ensure the x-axis reflects actual calendar months.
# All predicted values are on the original USD/lb scale for
# ARIMAX and MLR; ML model predictions are on the [0,1]
# Min-Max scaled range and are back-transformed here using
# the min and max of the full Arabica levels series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Actual test-set dates for Arabica
dates_test_ara <- df_arabica_levels$date[(n_train_ara_lev + 1):
                                          nrow(df_arabica_levels)]
dates_test_ara <- as.Date(paste0(dates_test_ara, "-01"))

# Actual observed prices (from ARIMAX result - identical across models)
actual_ara <- as.numeric(res_arimax_ara$actual)

# Back-transform ML predictions from [0,1] to USD/lb
# Min and Max are computed from the full levels dataset
ara_min <- min(df_arabica_levels$arabica_price, na.rm = TRUE)
ara_max <- max(df_arabica_levels$arabica_price, na.rm = TRUE)

backtransform <- function(x_scaled, x_min, x_max) {
  x_scaled * (x_max - x_min) + x_min
}

df_forecasts_ara <- data.frame(
  date   = rep(dates_test_ara, 6),
  actual = rep(actual_ara, 6),
  predicted = c(
    as.numeric(res_arimax_ara$predicted),
    as.numeric(res_mlr_ara$predicted),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_rf_ara$predicted),  ara_min, ara_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_xgb_ara$predicted), ara_min, ara_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_svm_ara$predicted), ara_min, ara_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_ann_ara$predicted), ara_min, ara_max)
  ),
  model = rep(c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"),
              each = length(dates_test_ara))
) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA — SAME STRUCTURE
# Robusta predictions are on USD/tonne for ARIMAX and MLR;
# ML predictions are back-transformed using Robusta min/max.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dates_test_rob <- df_robusta_levels$date[(n_train_rob_lev + 1):
                                          nrow(df_robusta_levels)]
dates_test_rob <- as.Date(paste0(dates_test_rob, "-01"))

actual_rob <- as.numeric(res_arimax_rob$actual)

rob_min <- min(df_robusta_levels$robusta_price, na.rm = TRUE)
rob_max <- max(df_robusta_levels$robusta_price, na.rm = TRUE)

df_forecasts_rob <- data.frame(
  date   = rep(dates_test_rob, 6),
  actual = rep(actual_rob, 6),
  predicted = c(
    as.numeric(res_arimax_rob$predicted),
    as.numeric(res_mlr_rob$predicted),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_rf_rob$predicted),  rob_min, rob_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_xgb_rob$predicted), rob_min, rob_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_svm_rob$predicted), rob_min, rob_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_ann_rob$predicted), rob_min, rob_max)
  ),
  model = rep(c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"),
              each = length(dates_test_rob))
) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX CONFIDENCE INTERVALS — ARABICA
# The forecast() function is re-called on the final ARIMAX
# model fitted on the full training set, using the test-set
# regressor matrix to generate h-step-ahead predictions
# with 95% confidence intervals.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

xreg_test_ara <- as.matrix(
  df_arabica_levels[(n_train_ara_lev + 1):nrow(df_arabica_levels),
                    intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_arabica_levels))]
)

fc_ci_ara <- forecast(res_arimax_ara$model,
                      h     = nrow(xreg_test_ara),
                      xreg  = xreg_test_ara,
                      level = 95)

df_ci_ara <- data.frame(
  date  = dates_test_ara,
  lower = as.numeric(fc_ci_ara$lower[, "95%"]),
  upper = as.numeric(fc_ci_ara$upper[, "95%"])
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX CONFIDENCE INTERVALS — ROBUSTA
# Same procedure applied to the Robusta series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

xreg_test_rob <- as.matrix(
  df_robusta_levels[(n_train_rob_lev + 1):nrow(df_robusta_levels),
                    intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_robusta_levels))]
)

fc_ci_rob <- forecast(res_arimax_rob$model,
                      h     = nrow(xreg_test_rob),
                      xreg  = xreg_test_rob,
                      level = 95)

df_ci_rob <- data.frame(
  date  = dates_test_rob,
  lower = as.numeric(fc_ci_rob$lower[, "95%"]),
  upper = as.numeric(fc_ci_rob$upper[, "95%"])
)
```

#### Actual vs Predicted — Arabica

*This chunk produces the six-panel actual vs predicted plot for Arabica. Each panel corresponds to one model; the black line shows observed prices and the coloured line shows the walk-forward forecasts over the test period. A close alignment between the two lines indicates strong predictive performance; systematic gaps or phase shifts reveal structural weaknesses in the model.*

```{r forecast_plots_arabica, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}

# R² labels to display inside each panel
r2_labels_ara <- metriques_all %>%
  filter(Series == "Arabica") %>%
  mutate(R2    = as.numeric(R2),
         label = paste0("R² = ", round(R2, 3))) %>%
  select(model = Model, label) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))

ggplot(df_forecasts_ara, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = df_forecasts_ara %>%
      filter(model == "ARIMAX") %>%
      left_join(df_ci_ara, by = "date"),
    aes(x = date, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill        = "#8B4513",
    alpha       = 0.12,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual), color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted), color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.8,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_label(data = r2_labels_ara,
             aes(label = label),
             x         = min(df_forecasts_ara$date) + 30,
             y         = max(df_forecasts_ara$actual) * 0.97,
             hjust     = 0, size = 2.8, fontface = "bold",
             fill      = "white", linewidth = 0, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title    = "Actual vs Predicted — Arabica futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Black: observed price (USD/lb)  |  Dashed brown: model forecast  |  Shaded band: ARIMAX 95% CI",
       x = NULL, y = "USD/lb") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")
```

The Arabica forecast trajectories confirm and nuance the aggregate $R^2$ metrics reported in the comparative table. ARIMAX and XGBoost track the observed price most closely throughout the test period, capturing both the gradual rise through 2021–2022 and the subsequent decline, consistent with their near-identical $R^2$ values of 0.821 and 0.818 respectively. Both models tend to lag slightly at turning points, a pattern typical of one-step-ahead walk-forward forecasts where the model has not yet observed the reversal. The 95% confidence interval displayed for ARIMAX widens progressively over the test period, reflecting the growing uncertainty of multi-step extrapolation from the training-set model. The observed price stays within the confidence band for the large majority of the test period, with only minor excursions at the sharpest turning points.

MLR follows the broad trend reasonably well but produces smoother forecasts that miss the amplitude of short-term fluctuations, reflecting the absence of any autoregressive component in its specification. Random Forest behaves similarly, with forecasts that track the trend but compress the peaks and troughs relative to the observed series, a consequence of the averaging across 500 trees that attenuates extreme predictions.

The SVM panel shows forecasts that broadly track the observed price, with the tuned hyperparameters ($cost = 5$, $gamma = 0.05$) producing a reasonable fit across most of the test period.

The ANN panel is the most striking: while the model tracks the general direction of price movements, it produces a pronounced upward spike around mid-2022 that reaches approximately 3.5 USD/lb against an observed price of around 2.5 USD/lb. This instability arises from the random weight reinitialisation at each walk-forward step in `nnet`, with only approximately 170 training observations at the early test steps, leaving the network susceptible to converging to local minima that produce extreme predictions for isolated observations. This explains the lower $R^2$ of 0.453 relative to the other models and is discussed further in the limitations section.

#### Actual vs Predicted — Robusta

*This chunk produces the equivalent six-panel plot for Robusta. The shorter test period (approximately 39 months) makes the visual comparison more compressed, but the same alignment logic applies. The sharp upward trend visible from 2022 onward is a key diagnostic: models that fail to track this trend will show a pronounced divergence in the right portion of each panel.*

```{r forecast_plots_robusta, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}

# R² labels to display inside each panel
r2_labels_rob <- metriques_all %>%
  filter(Series == "Robusta") %>%
  mutate(R2    = as.numeric(R2),
         label = paste0("R² = ", round(R2, 3))) %>%
  select(model = Model, label) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))

ggplot(df_forecasts_rob, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = df_forecasts_rob %>%
      filter(model == "ARIMAX") %>%
      left_join(df_ci_rob, by = "date"),
    aes(x = date, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill        = "#2E8B57",
    alpha       = 0.12,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual), color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted), color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 0.8,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_label(data = r2_labels_rob,
             aes(label = label),
             x         = min(df_forecasts_rob$date) + 30,
             y         = max(df_forecasts_rob$actual) * 0.97,
             hjust     = 0, size = 2.8, fontface = "bold",
             fill      = "white", linewidth = 0, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title    = "Actual vs Predicted — Robusta futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Black: observed price (USD/tonne)  |  Dashed green: model forecast  |  Shaded band: ARIMAX 95% CI",
       x = NULL, y = "USD/tonne") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")
```

The Robusta forecast trajectories reveal a more heterogeneous picture than Arabica. ARIMAX stands out as the strongest model, with its dashed line tracking the observed price closely throughout the test period, including the sharp upward surge from 2023, consistent with its $R^2$ of 0.929. The 95% confidence interval for ARIMAX is notably wider than its Arabica counterpart, reflecting the substantially higher residual variance of the Robusta model ($\sigma^2 = 6{,}270$ vs 0.005 for Arabica) and the greater uncertainty inherent in forecasting a strongly trending and volatile series. Despite this width, the observed price remains within the confidence band for almost the entire test period. The progressive widening of the band toward the end of the test period is consistent with the growing uncertainty of autoregressive forecasts over longer horizons.

MLR fails visibly, with forecasts oscillating erratically around the observed series and producing large directional errors in both 2022 and 2024. This confirms that a static linear specification without temporal dynamics cannot capture the persistent upward trend that dominates the Robusta test period, and explains its $R^2$ of 0.276.

Among the ML models, XGBoost tracks the broad trajectory reasonably well ($R^2$ = 0.796) but underestimates the acceleration visible from mid-2023 onward, with the dashed line flattening while the observed price continues rising sharply. Random Forest shows a similar pattern with a slightly lower fit ($R^2$ = 0.695). Both models appear to anchor on the historical price range seen during training, struggling to extrapolate beyond it, a pattern consistent with the known tendency of tree-based ensemble methods to compress predictions toward the training distribution.

The SVM panel shows oscillations throughout the test period, with forecast lines diverging from the observed series at several points. The ANN panel exhibits a more pronounced instability, with a prominent upward spike visible in early 2022, mirroring the pattern observed for Arabica and confirming that the instability of `nnet` weight initialisation is a structural limitation under the current walk-forward configuration with a small training window.

### Forecast Residuals

*This chunk plots the forecast residuals (predicted minus actual) for each model over the test period. A residual series hovering around zero with no systematic pattern indicates an unbiased model; persistent positive or negative deviations reveal directional bias, while increasing variance over time suggests heteroskedasticity in the forecast errors. Note that the y-axis scale varies freely across panels to accommodate the different magnitudes of Arabica and Robusta residuals.*

```{r residuals_plots, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}

df_residuals <- bind_rows(
  df_forecasts_ara %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Arabica"),
  df_forecasts_rob %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Robusta")
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT 1 — ARABICA RESIDUALS
# Fixed y-axis scale across all panels to allow direct
# comparison of residual amplitude between models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_res_ara <- ggplot(
  df_residuals %>% filter(series == "Arabica"),
  aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ifelse(residual > 0, 0, residual),
                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),
              fill = "#8B4513", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(title    = "Forecast residuals — Arabica futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Residual = Predicted - Actual. Dashed line at zero.",
       x = NULL, y = "Residual (USD/lb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT 2 — ROBUSTA RESIDUALS
# Fixed y-axis scale across all panels to allow direct
# comparison of residual amplitude between models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

p_res_rob <- ggplot(
  df_residuals %>% filter(series == "Robusta"),
  aes(x = date, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = ifelse(residual > 0, 0, residual),
                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),
              fill = "#2E8B57", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(title    = "Forecast residuals — Robusta futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Residual = Predicted - Actual. Dashed line at zero.",
       x = NULL, y = "Residual (USD/tonne)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")

p_res_ara
p_res_rob
```

The residual plots complement the forecast trajectory analysis by making directional biases and error patterns explicitly visible. Within each variety, the y-axis scale is fixed across all panels to allow direct comparison of residual amplitude between models.

**For Arabica**, ARIMAX, XGBoost and SVM produce the cleanest residuals, oscillating symmetrically around zero throughout the test period. MLR and Random Forest both show a pronounced negative spike around 2022, reflecting the lag at the peak of the price cycle. The ANN panel exhibits the largest amplitude of any Arabica model, with alternating positive and negative spikes in 2022 and 2023, consistent with the instability of `nnet` weight reinitialisation documented in the trajectory analysis.

**For Robusta**, ARIMAX produces the most well-behaved residuals, oscillating symmetrically around zero with no persistent sign pattern. MLR shows a pronounced negative episode beginning in mid-2022, persisting through the end of the test period, confirming the directional failure already visible in the forecast trajectory plot. Random Forest exhibits a persistent negative bias from mid-2022 onward. XGBoost shows a negative episode in 2021 that reverts toward zero, followed by a renewed negative bias from late 2022 that accentuates through 2023 before partially recovering. Both patterns are consistent with the extrapolation limitation of tree-based ensemble methods noted in the trajectory analysis. SVM shows oscillations of moderate amplitude throughout the test period, with no persistent directional bias. The ANN panel exhibits a prominent positive spike in early 2021, after which residuals revert toward zero, suggesting the instability is localised rather than systematic.

## Robustness Check: Disaggregated Climate Variables

The main model specifications rely on two production-weighted climate indices that aggregate temperature and precipitation conditions across 14 producer countries into single monthly series. While this aggregation is methodologically motivated, as it avoids endogeneity, reduces dimensionality, and is consistent with the fixed-weight approach documented in the data section, it raises the question of whether relevant country-specific climate information is lost in the process.

To assess this, the four ML models are re-estimated under an alternative specification in which the two aggregated indices are replaced by the 28 individual national series (14 countries × 2 climate variables), holding all other predictors constant. A comparison of out-of-sample $R^2$ between the two configurations provides direct evidence on whether disaggregation improves predictive accuracy. ARIMAX and MLR are excluded from this comparison: ARIMAX is computationally prohibitive with 40 regressors in a walk-forward loop, and MLR is ill-conditioned with 40 predictors on approximately 170 training observations.

*The chunk below re-estimates the four ML models using the disaggregated variable list and stores the results for comparison with the baseline specification. The model functions are identical in structure to those used in the main results, with a `vars_exo_vec` argument replacing the global `vars_exo` list.*

```{r robustness_disaggregated, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — LOAD THE DISAGGREGATED CLIMATE SERIES AND BUILD
# THE DISAGGREGATED DATASET
# The two production-weighted indices (indice_precip,
# indice_temp) are dropped from the monthly dataset and
# replaced by the 28 individual national series, 14 for
# precipitation and 14 for temperature.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_precip_dis <- read_csv(
  file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "precip_disaggregated_2000_2023.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)

df_temp_dis <- read_csv(
  file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "temp_disaggregated_2000_2023.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)

dataset_disagg <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  select(-indice_precip, -indice_temp) %>%
  left_join(df_precip_dis, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(df_temp_dis,   by = "date")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — DEFINE THE DISAGGREGATED EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LIST
# vars_climate_dis lists the 28 national climate columns
# (precip_bresil, precip_vietnam, ..., temp_bresil, ...).
# vars_exo_dis replaces indice_precip and indice_temp in the
# baseline vars_exo list with these 28 columns, keeping the
# other 12 baseline predictors unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_climate_dis <- c(
  paste0("precip_", names(POIDS_PRODUCTION)),
  paste0("temp_",   names(POIDS_PRODUCTION))
)

vars_exo_dis <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
  "ending_stocks", "oni", "cot_net_mm",
  vars_climate_dis
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — PREPARE THE DISAGGREGATED DATASETS
# Same logic as preparer_niveaux() in the preprocessing chunk:
# keep the dependent variable and the 40 exogenous predictors,
# drop rows with any missing value, and sort by date.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux_dis <- function(df, var_dep) {
  colonnes_a_garder <- c("date", var_dep, vars_exo_dis)
  df_modele         <- df[, colonnes_a_garder]
  df_modele         <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele[order(df_modele$date), ]
}

df_arabica_dis <- preparer_niveaux_dis(dataset_disagg, "arabica_price")
df_robusta_dis <- preparer_niveaux_dis(
  dataset_disagg[!is.na(dataset_disagg$robusta_price), ], "robusta_price")

n_train_ara_dis <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_dis) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_dis <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_dis) * split_ratio)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — GENERIC MODEL FUNCTIONS
# Identical in structure to the main model functions, with
# an added vars_exo_vec argument so the same function can
# be reused with different predictor lists without copying
# the function body.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_rf_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    foret <- randomForest(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                          ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
    predictions[i] <- predict(foret, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_xgb_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  colonnes_predicteurs <- setdiff(colnames(df_modele_scaled), var_dep)
  X       <- as.matrix(df_modele_scaled[, colonnes_predicteurs])
  y       <- df_modele_scaled[[var_dep]]
  n_total <- length(y)
  n_test  <- n_total - n_train

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    indices_fenetre  <- 1:(n_train + i - 1)
    indice_a_predire <- n_train + i
    modele_xgb <- xgboost(data      = X[indices_fenetre, ],
                          label     = y[indices_fenetre],
                          nrounds   = 100, max_depth = 4,
                          eta       = 0.1, subsample = 0.8,
                          verbose   = 0,
                          objective = "reg:squarederror")
    ligne_a_predire <- matrix(X[indice_a_predire, ], nrow = 1)
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_xgb, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  list(actual = y[(n_train + 1):n_total], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_svm_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_svm <- svm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                      kernel = "radial", cost = 1, gamma = 0.1)
    predictions[i] <- predict(modele_svm, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_ann_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  set.seed(42)
  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ann <- nnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                       size = 5, linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)
    predictions[i] <- predict(modele_ann, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — RUN ALL FOUR MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running disaggregated RF - Arabica...\n")
res_rf_dis_ara  <- fit_rf_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated RF - Robusta...\n")
res_rf_dis_rob  <- fit_rf_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)

cat("Running disaggregated XGBoost - Arabica...\n")
res_xgb_dis_ara <- fit_xgb_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated XGBoost - Robusta...\n")
res_xgb_dis_rob <- fit_xgb_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)

cat("Running disaggregated SVM - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_dis_ara <- fit_svm_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated SVM - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_dis_rob <- fit_svm_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)

cat("Running disaggregated ANN - Arabica...\n")
res_ann_dis_ara <- fit_ann_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated ANN - Robusta...\n")
res_ann_dis_rob <- fit_ann_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 6 — COMPILE RESULTS INTO A COMPARISON TABLE
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_robustness <- data.frame(
  Model  = rep(c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"), each = 2),
  Series = rep(c("Arabica", "Robusta"), 4),
  R2_baseline = as.numeric(c(
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "Random Forest", Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "Random Forest", Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "XGBoost",       Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "XGBoost",       Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "SVM",           Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "SVM",           Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "ANN",           Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "ANN",           Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2)
  )),
  R2_disaggregated = c(
    calculer_metriques(res_rf_dis_ara$actual,  res_rf_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_rf_dis_rob$actual,  res_rf_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_xgb_dis_ara$actual, res_xgb_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_xgb_dis_rob$actual, res_xgb_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_svm_dis_ara$actual, res_svm_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_svm_dis_rob$actual, res_svm_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_ann_dis_ara$actual, res_ann_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_ann_dis_rob$actual, res_ann_dis_rob$predicted)$R2
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2         = round(R2_disaggregated - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline      = round(R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_disaggregated = round(R2_disaggregated, 4)
  )
```

*The table below compares the out-of-sample $R^2$ of each model under the baseline aggregated specification and the disaggregated specification. A positive $ΔR^2$ indicates that disaggregation improves predictive accuracy; a negative value indicates deterioration.*

```{r robustness_table}

df_robustness %>%
  arrange(Series, Model) %>%
  select(Model, R2_baseline, R2_disaggregated, Delta_R2) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Robustness check — aggregated vs disaggregated climate indices (out-of-sample R²)",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R² (aggregated)",
                      "R² (disaggregated)", "ΔR²")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(4, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 5, 8,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(
    df_robustness %>% arrange(Series, Model) %>% pull(Delta_R2) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))
```

The robustness check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification. Disaggregation systematically deteriorates out-of-sample $R^2$ across all four ML models and both coffee varieties, with every $ΔR^2$ value negative. The deterioration is moderate for Random Forest ($ΔR^2$ of −0.044 for Arabica, −0.115 for Robusta) and XGBoost (−0.020 and −0.058), but severe for SVM and ANN, which produce negative $R^2$ values under the disaggregated specification, indicating performance worse than a naive mean forecast.

This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality: with 40 regressors and approximately 170 training observations, models sensitive to input dimensionality become severely overparameterised and fail to generalise to the test period. The ensemble methods Random Forest and XGBoost are more robust to this problem through their built-in variable selection mechanisms, but still suffer a meaningful performance loss. These results suggest that the production-weighted aggregation improves the climate signal by filtering out country-specific noise, and that the information gain from disaggregation is outweighed by the dimensionality cost at the sample sizes available in this study.

## Variety-Specific Model Specification

The robustness check conducted in the preceding section validated the production-weighted aggregation methodology by showing that disaggregated climate indices systematically deteriorate out-of-sample performance. A second robustness check is now conducted by re-estimating all six models under a variety-specific specification. Rather than using global climate indices and world supply-and-demand fundamentals, this specification assigns each model its own set of variety-relevant predictors: the Arabica models use climate indices and fundamentals aggregated across the ten Arabica-producing countries, while the Robusta models use the equivalent aggregates for the six Robusta-producing countries. This specification is motivated by the structural concentration of Robusta production in Vietnam and Indonesia (approximately 67% combined) and the broader geographic diversification of Arabica production. Using global indices for Robusta in particular dilutes the climate and supply signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually no Robusta.

*This chunk defines the variety-specific exogenous variable lists and prepares the two datasets used in the re-estimation below. Sample sizes are printed to the console for verification.*

```{r preprocessing_vs, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VARIETY-SPECIFIC EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LISTS
# Two separate lists replace the global vars_exo: one for
# Arabica models (climate indices and fundamentals aggregated
# across the 10 Arabica-producing countries) and one for
# Robusta models (aggregated across the 6 Robusta-producing
# countries). All other predictors (sugar, cocoa, macro
# variables, ONI, COT) are unchanged from the baseline.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo_ara_vs <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production_ara", "consumption", "exports",
  "ending_stocks_ara", "indice_precip_arabica", "indice_temp_arabica",
  "oni", "cot_net_mm"
)

vars_exo_rob_vs <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production_rob", "consumption", "exports",
  "ending_stocks_rob", "indice_precip_robusta", "indice_temp_robusta",
  "oni", "cot_net_mm"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PREPARE THE VARIETY-SPECIFIC DATASETS
# Same logic as preparer_niveaux() used throughout the
# document: keep the dependent variable and the relevant
# exogenous predictors, drop rows with any missing value,
# and sort by date.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux_vs <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec) {
  colonnes_a_garder <- c("date", var_dep, vars_exo_vec)
  df_modele         <- df[, colonnes_a_garder]
  df_modele         <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele[order(df_modele$date), ]
}

df_arabica_vs <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_arabica_vs, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara_vs)

df_robusta_vs <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_robusta_vs[!is.na(dataset_robusta_vs$robusta_price), ],
  "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob_vs)

# 80/20 split, using the same split_ratio as every other model
n_train_ara_vs <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_vs) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_vs <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_vs) * split_ratio)

cat("Arabica VS - Train:", n_train_ara_vs,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_vs) - n_train_ara_vs, "\n")
cat("Robusta VS - Train:", n_train_rob_vs,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_vs) - n_train_rob_vs, "\n")
```

Sample sizes for the variety-specific datasets mirror those of the baseline specification, 168 training and 43 test observations for Arabica, and 153 training and 39 test observations for Robusta, confirming that the variety-specific variable substitution does not alter the temporal coverage of either dataset.

All six models are re-estimated under this specification using the same walk-forward protocol as the baseline. The Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM and ANN models reuse the generic functions already defined in the disaggregated robustness check above, called here with the variety-specific variable lists. ARIMAX and MLR are generalised below by adding a `vars_exo_vec` argument following the same pattern.

*The chunk below defines the generic ARIMAX and MLR functions and re-estimates all six models under the variety-specific specification.*

```{r modeles_vs, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — GENERIC ARIMAX FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_arimax() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec rather than
# always using the global vars_exo. This allows the function
# to be called with any predictor list without modification.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo_vec])

  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  n_total    <- length(serie_dependante)
  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]
  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test     <- length(y_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1
    indices_vus          <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu                 <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu              <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]
    y_fenetre            <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre         <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      auto.arima(y_fenetre, xreg = xreg_fenetre,
                 stepwise = TRUE, approximation = TRUE,
                 max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) { predictions[i] <- NA; next }

    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  list(actual = y_test, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — GENERIC MLR FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_mlr() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec. intersect()
# ensures only columns present in df are used, guarding
# against any name mismatch between the variable list and
# the dataset columns.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_mlr_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele)
  donnees_train <- df_modele[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ols           <- lm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement)
    predictions[i]       <- predict(modele_ols, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — RUN ALL SIX MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# Each model is called twice: once for Arabica using
# df_arabica_vs and vars_exo_ara_vs, and once for Robusta
# using df_robusta_vs and vars_exo_rob_vs. The four ML
# generic functions were defined in the disaggregated
# robustness check chunk and are reused here unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Arabica...\n")
res_arimax_ara_vs <- fit_arimax_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                          vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Robusta...\n")
res_arimax_rob_vs <- fit_arimax_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                          vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific MLR - Arabica...\n")
res_mlr_ara_vs <- fit_mlr_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific MLR - Robusta...\n")
res_mlr_rob_vs <- fit_mlr_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific RF - Arabica...\n")
res_rf_ara_vs <- fit_rf_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                  vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific RF - Robusta...\n")
res_rf_rob_vs <- fit_rf_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                  vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific XGBoost - Arabica...\n")
res_xgb_ara_vs <- fit_xgb_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific XGBoost - Robusta...\n")
res_xgb_rob_vs <- fit_xgb_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific SVM - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_ara_vs <- fit_svm_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific SVM - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_rob_vs <- fit_svm_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific ANN - Arabica...\n")
res_ann_ara_vs <- fit_ann_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific ANN - Robusta...\n")
res_ann_rob_vs <- fit_ann_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — STACK PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to each model's actual and
# predicted vectors. Results are stacked into a single 12-row
# data frame (6 models × 2 series) and numeric columns are
# coerced from character to numeric as in metriques_all.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_vs_all <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara_vs$actual, res_arimax_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob_vs$actual, res_arimax_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_ara_vs$actual, res_mlr_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_rob_vs$actual, res_mlr_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara_vs$actual, res_rf_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob_vs$actual, res_rf_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_ara_vs$actual, res_xgb_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_rob_vs$actual, res_xgb_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara_vs$actual, res_svm_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob_vs$actual, res_svm_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara_vs$actual, res_ann_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob_vs$actual, res_ann_rob_vs$predicted))
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))
```

*The table and chart below compare the out-of-sample $R^2$ of each model under the baseline and variety-specific specifications. A positive $ΔR^2$ indicates improvement under the variety-specific specification; a negative value indicates deterioration.*

```{r comparative_vs, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(ggh4x)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — BUILD THE COMPARISON DATA FRAME
# The baseline R² from metriques_all is joined to the
# variety-specific R² from metriques_vs_all. Delta_R2 is
# the difference between the two, positive values indicating
# improvement under the variety-specific specification.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_comparison_vs <- metriques_all %>%
  select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
  mutate(R2 = as.numeric(R2)) %>%
  rename(R2_baseline = R2) %>%
  left_join(
    metriques_vs_all %>%
      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_vs = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2    = round(R2_vs - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline = round(R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_vs       = round(R2_vs, 4)
  )


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — DISPLAY THE COMPARISON TABLE
# Models are sorted by decreasing baseline R² within each
# series. pack_rows() adds colour-coded group headers for
# Arabica and Robusta. The Delta_R2 column is coloured green
# for positive values and red for negative values.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_comparison_vs %>%
  arrange(Series, desc(R2_baseline)) %>%
  select(Model, R2_baseline, R2_vs, Delta_R2) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Baseline vs variety-specific specification — out-of-sample R²",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R² (baseline)",
                      "R² (variety-specific)", "ΔR²")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(6, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 6,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 7, 12,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(
    df_comparison_vs %>%
      arrange(Series, desc(R2_baseline)) %>%
      pull(Delta_R2) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — BAR CHART
# Models are ordered by decreasing baseline R² to match the
# table ordering. The two specifications are shown side by
# side within each model, faceted by coffee variety.
# facet_wrap2() from ggh4x allows different strip background
# colours per panel, using Arabica brown and Robusta green
# consistent with the palette used throughout the document.
# geom_text() adds R² labels above each bar for readability.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_vs_all %>%
  mutate(Specification = "Variety-specific") %>%
  bind_rows(
    metriques_all %>%
      mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric),
             Specification = "Baseline")
  ) %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(Model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "XGBoost", "SVM",
                                   "Random Forest", "MLR", "ANN"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = R2, fill = Specification)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge",
           alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 3)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 2.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Baseline"         = "#95A5A6",
                               "Variety-specific" = "#2E5090")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.05),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  facet_wrap2(~ Series, ncol = 2,
              strip = strip_themed(
                background_x = list(
                  element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6"),
                  element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec")
                ),
                text_x = list(
                  element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, color = "#8B4513"),
                  element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, color = "#2E8B57")
                )
              )) +
  labs(title = "Baseline vs variety-specific specification — out-of-sample R²",
       x = NULL, y = expression(R^2), fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )
```

The variety-specific specification yields asymmetric results across the two coffee varieties, revealing an important structural difference in how variety-relevant climate and supply information contributes to predictive accuracy.
